paras: The threatened lynching of David James was a manhunt near Aspen, Colorado, in early May 1888, in which a posse pursued James, accused of assaulting a young neighbor girl, with the declared intention of lynching him if he was caught. No lynching was reported, and a brief notice a few days later said James was in jail.

According to a dispatch from Aspen, James was a ranchman of about thirty-five who lived near Emma Station, next to a family named Ellison. No article gives the race of James, the girl or the pursuers.

The first wire report, dated Aspen, May 6, said James had "criminally assaulted an eight year old girl named Ellison" the day before and escaped. The Omaha Bee's dispatch of May 8 gave the girl's age as six and said James had enticed her into his cabin. Accounts of her condition ranged from "critical" to dying.

James fled to the mountains, pursued by what the early wire called a posse and the Omaha dispatch called settlers. Both versions stated that he would be lynched if captured, the Omaha text adding that he "will surely be lynched."

On May 10 the Wyoming Tribune reported in a single line that James was "in jail." The coverage does not show how or where he was captured, whether a crowd gathered at the jail, or whether he was tried.

The story ran as a short telegraphic item in distant papers on May 7, headed "Will Lynch Him" in the Memphis Appeal and "Will be Lynched if Caught" over a Denver dateline in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, while the Washington Critic carried the same text without a heading. The Omaha Bee printed its longer version under the headline "A Ranchman's Heinous Crime." Every report stated the accusation as fact and treated the expected lynching as a matter of course, without comment.

The reports differ on the girl's age, eight or six, and on the date: the Omaha dispatch's "yesterday" would place the assault on May 7, after the story had already appeared in print, so the May 5 date of the first wire is the better supported.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of David James
bases: The only collective action reported is a posse or settlers pursuing an accused man whom, the dispatches said, they would lynch if captured (A1, A4); no attack on him is reported, and a later brief says he was in jail (A5).

No one was reported killed: the papers report only a pursuit and a predicted lynching (A1, A2, A4), and the last report has James in jail (A5). The size and authority of the posse or 'settlers' are not given.

Two differently worded dispatches, an Aspen May 6 wire (A1, with the Denver version A2/A3) and a fuller Aspen May 8 dispatch (A4), agree on the accusation, the escape, the pursuit and the threat, though they may share an Aspen source; only A5 reports the capture.

accounts.label: Aspen/Denver wire, May 6-7
accounts.gist: James criminally assaulted an eight-year-old girl named Ellison and fled; a posse was after him and he would be lynched if caught; the girl was critical or dying.

accounts.label: Aspen dispatch, May 8
accounts.gist: James, a thirty-five-year-old ranchman near Emma Station, enticed his neighbor's six-year-old daughter into his cabin and assaulted her, then escaped to the mountains; settlers were in pursuit and would 'surely' lynch him.

framing.detail: Short telegraphic items headed 'Will Lynch Him' and 'Will be Lynched if Caught' stated the accusation as fact and reported the expected lynching without comment.
The Omaha Bee headed its fuller dispatch 'A Ranchman's Heinous Crime' and said James 'will surely be lynched' if captured.
The Wyoming Tribune called James 'an Aspen, Colo., child rapist' in a one-line local item.

conflicts.note: The earlier date is better supported: the story was already in print on May 7 (A1, A2), so the May 8 dispatch's 'yesterday' is probably carried over from an earlier text.
No later report of her condition was found.
Neither says whether officers led or deputized the pursuers.
